mainTopic: Liability for damage in a shared courtyard: רבי אלעזר, רב יוסף's ברייתא, and רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's four rules
overview: This amud finishes explaining a ברייתא about a borrowed ox. In the first case, the borrower never took on the job of stopping the ox from causing damage. The second half of that ברייתא is a different case, where he did take on that job. The גמרא then challenges רבי אלעזר, who exempts partners for שן and רגל in a shared courtyard, using a ברייתא of רב יוסף that makes them liable. רבי אלעזר answers that the ברייתות disagree, and he quotes רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's four rules, which exempt partners in a shared courtyard. The גמרא settles the clash: one courtyard is set aside for both produce and oxen, while the other is set aside only for produce. רבי זירא and אביי then argue whether a produce-only courtyard counts as 'another's field'. Next the גמרא studies the four rules closely. It reads 'חייב בכל' as full damage, following רבי טרפון, and asks whether the last rule switches to the רבנן. רבינא offers a reading where the whole ברייתא follows רבי טרפון. The גמרא objects that this leaves only three rules, and רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer begins at the very end of the amud and continues on the next one.

steps.title: The borrower did not take on guarding against damage
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of an answer: in the ברייתא's case, the borrower did not take on the job of stopping the ox from causing damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...but he did not take upon himself the job of guarding it from causing damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it started just before this point. It explains that the borrower in the ברייתא did not agree to stop the lender's ox from causing damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the borrower never took on that job, the responsibility for the ox's damage stays with the owner, the משאיל. That lets the ברייתא be read in a way that fits the earlier discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: took upon himself, agreed to be responsible for
guarding the animal so it does not cause damage
a borrower
a lender (here, the ox's owner)

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different kinds of guarding. Guarding the ox so nothing happens to it is one job. Guarding it so it does not hurt others (שמירת נזקיו) is another job. A borrower can take on one without the other.

phrases.english: but he did not take upon himself the guarding of its damages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from just before this point, which defined the case of the ברייתא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the borrower did not take on responsibility for the ox's damage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower is responsible for anything the ox does
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the job of guarding against damage makes the borrower responsible, and here he did not take it on

steps.title: The second half of the ברייתא implies the borrower can be liable
steps.stepSummary: If the borrower never took on guarding against damage, why does the סיפא suggest he is liable when the wall broke open by day?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the second half: if the wall broke open at night, or robbers broke it open, and the ox went out and caused damage, he is exempt. That implies that if it broke open by day, he is liable. But he never took on the job of guarding against its damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 1. It points out that the second half of the same ברייתא seems to make the borrower liable in some cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא exempts him only for a break-in at night or by robbers. From this we learn that a break-in by day would make him liable. But if he never took on guarding against damage, he should never be liable at all, so the explanation in step 1 does not seem to fit.

keyTerms.meaning: if so, if that is the case
the latter part of a source
it (the enclosure) broke open
robbers, bandits
this implies; but look

phrases.english: If so, say the latter clause:
if it broke open at night, or robbers broke it open,
phrases.notes: "It" is the wall or fence that was keeping the ox in.

phrases.english: and it went out and caused damage, he is exempt.
This implies: by day, he is liable?

phrases.aramaic: הָא לֹא קִבֵּל עָלָיו שְׁמִירַת נְזָקָיו!
phrases.english: But he did not take upon himself the guarding of its damages!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation given in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the borrower in the ברייתא did not take on guarding against damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא implies the borrower is liable for a daytime break-in, which only makes sense if he did take on guarding against damage

steps.title: The second half is talking about a borrower who did take on that job
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא is a new case: if the borrower did take on guarding against damage, he is liable, except for a break-in at night or by robbers.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: if he did take on guarding against its damage, he is liable. But if the wall broke open at night, or robbers broke it open, and the ox went out and caused damage, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the second half of the ברייתא is not the same case as the first half. It is talking about a borrower who did agree to guard against damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half is a borrower who did not take on guarding against damage, so he is not liable. The second half is a borrower who did take it on, so he is liable. Even he is exempt when the break-in was not his fault, like at night or by robbers. This keeps step 1's reading of the first half.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it means to say
liable, must pay
exempt, does not pay

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא has two cases. A borrower who did not take on guarding against damage is not liable. A borrower who did take it on is liable, unless the break-in was beyond his control.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:

phrases.aramaic: אִם קִבֵּל עָלָיו שְׁמִירַת נְזָקָיו – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: if he took upon himself the guarding of its damages, he is liable.
If it broke open at night, or robbers broke it open,
and it went out and caused damage, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the ברייתא into two separate cases (הכי קאמר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole ברייתא is about one borrower who did not take on guarding against damage
steps.terutzMaskana: The סיפא is about a borrower who did take on guarding against damage, so it can make him liable

steps.title: רב יוסף's ברייתא seems to refute רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף taught that in a partners' courtyard or an inn, one is liable for שן and רגל, against רבי אלעזר who exempts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? But רב יוסף taught: in a courtyard of partners, or an inn, one is liable for Eating and for Trampling. This refutes רבי אלעזר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי אלעזר's opinion and brings a new challenge against it. A ברייתא from רב יוסף says partners are liable for שן and רגל in a shared yard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר said that in a חצר השותפים, a partner whose animal causes שן or רגל damage is exempt. רב יוסף's ברייתא says the exact opposite, that he is liable. So it looks like a full refutation (תיובתא) of רבי אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (opens a challenge)
a courtyard shared by partners
an inn
Eating: damage done by an animal eating
Trampling: damage done by an animal walking
a refutation, a strong proof against someone's view

steps.whyThisMatters: A ברייתא is a stronger source than an אמורא like רבי אלעזר, so a direct contradiction like this is a serious problem for his view.

phrases.english: Is that so?! But didn't Rav Yosef teach:
phrases.notes: "That" is רבי אלעזר's ruling from earlier, that partners are exempt for שן and רגל in a shared yard.

phrases.english: a courtyard of partners, and an inn,

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בָּהֶן עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל.
phrases.english: one is liable in them for Eating and for Trampling.
A refutation of Rabbi Elazar!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the borrowed-ox discussion and goes back to challenge רבי אלעזר directly
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's ruling that partners are exempt for שן and רגל in a shared courtyard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יוסף's ברייתא says partners are liable for שן and רגל in a shared courtyard or inn, which directly contradicts רבי אלעזר

steps.title: רבי אלעזר answers that the ברייתות disagree
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר is not refuted by רב יוסף's ברייתא, because other ברייתות argue with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר could tell you: Do you really think that is a refutation? Don't the ברייתות disagree with each other on this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי אלעזר from the challenge in step 4. One ברייתא does not prove him wrong, because there are other ברייתות on his side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 used רב יוסף's ברייתא, which makes the owner liable for שן and רגל in a partners' courtyard, against רבי אלעזר. The answer is that this is a disagreement between תנאים. רבי אלעזר simply holds like the other ברייתא, which the גמרא is about to quote.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so? A push-back on the questioner's assumption
ברייתות, teachings of the תנאים not in the משנה
They disagree

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar could say to you:
And can you really think so?!
phrases.notes: He means: do you really think that one ברייתא settles the question against me?

phrases.english: Don't the ברייתות disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from רב יוסף's ברייתא in step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יוסף's ברייתא disproves רבי אלעזר.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי אלעזר follows a different ברייתא, so he is not refuted.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's four rules: the first two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא of four rules. In the victim's property the owner pays for everything, and in the damager's property he pays for nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר used to say four rules about damages. Any place that belongs to the victim and not to the damager: the damager is liable for everything. A place that belongs to the damager and not to the victim: he is exempt from everything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that backs up רבי אלעזר. This step gives its first two rules and sets up the third rule, which is the important one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The four rules are sorted by who has rights in the place where the damage happened. If only the victim has rights there, every kind of damage must be paid. If only the damager has rights there, nothing is paid, since the victim's things had no business being there.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was taught in a ברייתא, bringing a source
General rules
A תנא, the author of this ברייתא
The victim, the one who was damaged
The damager, here the owner of the animal that did the damage

phrases.english: And it was taught in a ברייתא:
Four rules

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר בְּנִזָּקִין:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would say about damages:
Any place that belongs to the victim
and not to the damager: he is liable for everything.
A place of the damager and not of the victim: he is exempt from everything.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא, אַרְבָּעָה כְּלָלוֹת הָיָה רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר בְּנִזָּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the disagreeing ברייתא that step 5 mentioned.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's ruling that the owner is exempt for שן and רגל in a shared courtyard.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's four rules (תוספתא).

steps.title: Third rule: a place belonging to both sides
steps.stepSummary: In a partners' courtyard or a valley, the owner is exempt for שן and רגל, but pays for the קרן-type damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: A place that belongs to both of them, like a partners' courtyard or a valley: he is exempt there for שן and רגל. For goring, pushing, biting, crouching, and kicking: a תם pays half damages, and a מועד pays full damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with its third rule. This is the rule that matches רבי אלעזר's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When both sides have rights in the place, eating and trampling are normal uses of a shared space, so the owner does not pay for them. The goring-type damages are still paid, half by a תם and full by a מועד, just like anywhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard shared by partners
A valley, an open field that several people use
An animal with no history of this damage; its owner pays half
An animal with a known habit of this damage; its owner pays in full

steps.confusionAlert: The exemption here is only for שן and רגל. For goring, biting, kicking and the like, the owner still pays even in a shared courtyard.

phrases.english: A place belonging to this one and to that one,
such as a partners' courtyard or a valley:

phrases.aramaic: פָּטוּר בָּהּ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל;
phrases.english: he is exempt there for Eating and for Trampling;
for goring and for pushing,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל הַנְּשִׁיכָה וְעַל הָרְבִיצָה וְעַל הַבְּעִיטָה –
phrases.english: and for biting, and for crouching, and for kicking:
an innocuous animal pays half damages,
a forewarned animal pays full damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָזֶה וְלָזֶה, כְּגוֹן חֲצַר הַשּׁוּתָּפִים וְהַבִּקְעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא with its third rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a place belonging to both sides, there is no liability for שן and רגל, but קרן-type damages are paid as usual.

steps.title: Fourth rule: a place belonging to neither side
steps.stepSummary: In a courtyard owned by neither of them, the owner is liable for שן and רגל, and the קרן-type damages are paid as usual.
steps.simpleTranslation: A place that belongs to neither of them, like a courtyard owned by neither: he is liable there for שן and רגל. For goring, biting, pushing, crouching, and kicking: a תם pays half damages, and a מועד pays full damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with its fourth rule, to complete the list of four.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here neither side owns the courtyard, and the ברייתא rules that the owner does pay for שן and רגל. So the exemption in the third rule depends on the damager having rights in the place. The קרן-type damages are paid the same in both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Which belongs to neither of the two
Full damages
Half damages

phrases.english: A place belonging neither to this one nor to that one,
such as a courtyard that belongs to neither of the two:

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בּוֹ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל;
phrases.english: he is liable there for Eating and for Trampling;
for goring and for biting,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל הַנְּגִיפָה וְעַל הָרְבִיצָה וְעַל הַבְּעִיטָה –
phrases.english: and for pushing, and for crouching, and for kicking:
an innocuous animal pays half damages,
a forewarned animal pays full damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה, כְּגוֹן חָצֵר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁל שְׁנֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the four rules of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a place belonging to neither side, the owner is liable for שן and רגל, and קרן-type damages are paid as usual.

steps.title: The point of the proof: exempt in a partners' courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to the third rule: in a partners' courtyard or a valley, the owner is exempt for שן and רגל, just as רבי אלעזר says.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches that in a partners' courtyard or a valley, he is exempt there for שן and רגל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks out the one line of the long ברייתא that matters. That line supports רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's ברייתא made the owner liable for שן and רגל in a partners' courtyard. This ברייתא makes him exempt. So this is a disagreement between ברייתות, and רבי אלעזר holds like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches. Used to point to the part of a source that proves the point

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר is not refuted by רב יוסף's ברייתא. The four rules of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר exempt the owner for שן and רגל in a partners' courtyard, so the ברייתות disagree.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the question of a shared courtyard is a disagreement between תנאים, so each אמורא can rely on a ברייתא.

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
a partners' courtyard or a valley:

phrases.aramaic: פָּטוּר בָּהּ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל;
phrases.english: he is exempt there for Eating and for Trampling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points to the line of the ברייתא from step 7 that proves רבי אלעזר's view.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's exemption for שן and רגל in a partners' courtyard.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The third rule of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ברייתא.

steps.title: The two ברייתות contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רב יוסף's ברייתא and the four-rule ברייתא give opposite rulings about a partners' courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: These two ברייתות contradict each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a clash between two sources. רב יוסף's ברייתא says the owner is liable for שן and רגל in a partners' courtyard, but the four-rule ברייתא says he is exempt there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 the גמרא used the four-rule ברייתא to support רבי אלעזר: exempt in a partners' courtyard. But רב יוסף's ברייתא says liable in that same kind of courtyard. Two ברייתות cannot give opposite rulings on the same case without an explanation, and the next step supplies one.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult; a problem
With each other; one against the other
A courtyard owned by partners

phrases.english: They are difficult against each other!
phrases.notes: He means רב יוסף's ברייתא (liable) and the four-rule ברייתא (exempt), both about a partners' courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 9 used the four-rule ברייתא to support רבי אלעזר. That now exposes a clash with רב יוסף's ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: How the two ברייתות fit together
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Same case (a partners' courtyard), opposite rulings for שן and רגל: one says liable, the other says exempt.

steps.title: Two different kinds of partners' courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The four-rule ברייתא is about a courtyard set aside for both produce and animals. רב יוסף's ברייתא is about a courtyard set aside only for produce, so for שן it counts as the victim's courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא (the four rules) is talking about a courtyard set aside for both partners, for produce and for oxen. רב יוסף's ברייתא is talking about a courtyard set aside for produce but not for oxen. So when it comes to eating damage (שן), it counts as the victim's courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying the two ברייתות describe different partnership terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both partners agreed to bring animals into the courtyard, an animal being there is allowed, so its owner is exempt. If they agreed only on produce, the animal has no right to be there. Toward the other partner's produce, the courtyard then works like the victim's own property, where the owner pays.

keyTerms.meaning: Set aside or designated for a certain use
Produce
Oxen; animals in general
The victim's courtyard, where the owner is fully liable

steps.confusionAlert: Both ברייתות are about a partners' courtyard. The difference is only in what the partners agreed the courtyard is for.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that liability for שן and רגל depends on whether the animal had a right to be in that place, not just on who owns the land.

phrases.english: When that one is taught,
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the four-rule ברייתא from step 6.

phrases.english: it is about a courtyard set aside for this one and that one,
both for produce and for oxen.
That one of רב יוסף
is about a courtyard set aside for produce,
but not set aside for oxen;
so with regard to eating damage,
it counts as the victim's courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ברייתא is about a different kind of courtyard.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות were thought to describe the same partners' courtyard.
steps.terutzMaskana: The four-rule ברייתא is about a courtyard set aside for produce and animals, so the owner is exempt. רב יוסף's ברייתא is about a courtyard set aside for produce only, so the owner is liable for שן.

steps.title: The wording of each ברייתא supports the split
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's ברייתא compares the courtyard to an inn, where animals don't belong. The other compares it to a valley, where animals do go. This proves the split is correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording is exact too. Here (רב יוסף's ברייתא) it lists the courtyard together with an inn, and there (the four-rule ברייתא) it lists it together with a valley. Learn from this that the answer is correct.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports its answer by showing that each ברייתא's own wording hints at the difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An inn is not a place for bringing in animals, so a courtyard grouped with an inn sounds like one set aside only for produce. A valley is open land where animals graze, so a courtyard grouped with a valley sounds like one where animals are allowed. The text itself matches the split from step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: The wording also shows this
An inn
A valley; open field land
Learn from it; this proves it

steps.whatToRemember: A partners' courtyard set aside for animals (like a valley) means exempt for שן and רגל. One set aside only for produce (like an inn) means liable for שן.

phrases.english: It is also precise,
since here it teaches it similar to an inn,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is רב יוסף's ברייתא, which lists the partners' courtyard alongside an inn.

phrases.english: and there it teaches it similar to a valley;
learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings textual support for the answer given in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: The split between a courtyard for produce only and one for produce and animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of the two ברייתות: one groups the courtyard with an inn (פונדק), the other with a valley (בקעה).

steps.title: רבי זירא: a shared courtyard is not 'another's field'
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא challenges the answer. If the courtyard is set aside for both partners' produce, it is not 'another's field', so there should be no liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא objected: Since the courtyard is set aside for produce, of both partners? But we need 'and it eats in another's field', and that is missing here!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא attacks the answer from step 11 for רב יוסף's ברייתא, using a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה makes the owner pay for שן when the animal eats 'in another's field'. In a courtyard set aside for both partners' produce, the animal's owner also has rights to the place, so it is not purely 'another's' field. That means liability should not apply, which undercuts the reading of רב יוסף's ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenges it
An אמורא who raises the objection
'And it eats in another's field', the פסוק about שן
We need; we require

phrases.english: רבי זירא challenged it:
Since it is set aside for produce?!
phrases.notes: He means set aside for both partners' produce, so the animal's owner has a share in the place too.

phrases.english: But we need 'and it eats in another's field',
and that is missing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer from step 11 after step 12 supported it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that רב יוסף's ברייתא is about a courtyard set aside only for produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק requires 'another's field' for שן. A courtyard shared for both partners' produce partly belongs to the animal's owner, so that condition is not met.

steps.title: אביי: a courtyard not meant for oxen counts as 'another's field'
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers רבי זירא. Since the courtyard is not set aside for oxen, the animal has no right to be there, so it counts as 'another's field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Since the courtyard is not set aside for oxen, we can call it 'another's field.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends the earlier answer against רבי זירא's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא argued that a courtyard belonging partly to the animal's owner can't be 'another's field.' אביי says ownership is not the key point. What matters is that the place is not set aside for animals. Since the ox doesn't belong there, the place counts as 'another's field' when it comes to שן.

keyTerms.meaning: 'another's field', the פסוק's wording for where שן and רגל are liable
set aside, designated (for a use)
I can call it, the term applies to it

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that for שן and רגל, 'another's field' depends on whether animals belong there, not only on who owns the land.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רבי זירא, who raised the challenge in the last step.

phrases.english: Since it is not set aside for oxen,
I can call it 'another's field.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: כֵּיוָן דְּאֵינָהּ מְיוּחֶדֶת לִשְׁווֹרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's challenge in step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the key term: 'another's field' means a place not set aside for the animal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי זירא thought a courtyard the owner partly owns cannot be 'another's field'
steps.terutzMaskana: Since oxen do not belong there, it counts as 'another's field', so the owner pays for שן

steps.title: Maybe the אמוראים don't argue either
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי asks רבינא: the two ברייתות turned out not to argue. Maybe the two אמוראים don't really argue either?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא of Difti said to רבינא: Should we say that just as the ברייתות don't argue, the אמוראים don't argue either?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the ברייתות have been explained as talking about different cases, רב אחא מדפתי asks whether the same fix works for the אמוראים' argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, two אמוראים seemed to argue about a partners' courtyard: one said the owner pays, and רבי אלעזר said he is exempt. The two ברייתות were just explained as covering two different kinds of courtyard. So maybe each אמורא is also talking about a different kind of courtyard, and there is no real argument.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say? (a suggestion)
the ברייתות (here, the two ברייתות discussed)
the אמוראים, the later scholars of the גמרא
they argue, disagree

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
Shall we say that since the ברייתות don't argue,
phrases.notes: These are רב יוסף's ברייתא and the four-rule ברייתא, explained in step 11 as covering different courtyards.

phrases.english: the אמוראים also don't argue?
phrases.notes: He means רב חסדא and רבי אלעזר, who argued earlier about a partners' courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא מִדְּמַתְנְיָתָא לָא פְּלִיגִי, אָמוֹרָאֵי נָמֵי לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the split between the ברייתות and applies it to the אמוראים' argument
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the אמוראים' argument can also be explained away as two different cases

steps.title: רבינא: Yes, or else they argue over רבי זירא versus אביי
steps.stepSummary: רבינא agrees that the אמוראים may not argue. He adds that if they do argue, their argument is the same as the one between רבי זירא and אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes. And if you want to say they do argue, they argue over רבי זירא's challenge and אביי's answer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the question. He agrees there may be no argument. If there is one, he shows exactly what it is about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two choices. First, the אמוראים don't argue at all, because each one is talking about a different kind of courtyard. Second, they argue only about a courtyard set aside for produce alone. One agrees with רבי זירא that it is not 'another's field,' so the owner is exempt. The other agrees with אביי that it is 'another's field,' so the owner pays.

keyTerms.meaning: yes
and if you want to say (a second possibility)
challenge, difficulty
answer, resolution

steps.whatToRemember: A partners' courtyard set aside for both produce and animals: the owner is exempt for שן and רגל. Set aside only for produce: אביי says the owner pays, because it counts as 'another's field.' רבי זירא says it does not count. The אמוראים may not argue at all, or they may argue the same way רבי זירא and אביי do.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.
And if you want to say they do argue,
over the challenge of Rabbi Zeira
and the answer of Abaye they argue.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין. וְאִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא מדפתי's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, the אמוראים may not argue. If they do, the argument is limited to a courtyard set aside for produce only, and matches the debate between רבי זירא and אביי.

steps.title: Back to the four rules: in the victim's property, the owner pays for everything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's four rules. The first rule: in a place that belongs to the victim and not to the one who did the damage, the owner pays for all damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the ברייתא itself: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר used to state four rules about damages. Any place that belongs to the victim and not to the one who did the damage, the owner is liable for everything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא it quoted earlier and starts going through it rule by rule. This step brings the first rule and sets up the analysis that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the victim's private property the animal has no right to be, so its owner is liable there. The exact wording 'חייב בכל' will matter: the next step shows it means he pays the full amount, not that he is liable for every type of damage.

keyTerms.meaning: 'the matter itself', a return to a source quoted earlier in order to study it
rules, principles
the victim, the one who was damaged
the one who did the damage (here, the animal's owner)
liable in all; the next step shows this means paying the full amount

phrases.english: The matter itself: four rules

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר בְּנִזָּקִין:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar used to state about damages:
Any place that belongs to the victim
and not to the one who did the damage,
he is liable for everything.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא – אַרְבָּעָה כְּלָלוֹת הָיָה רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר בְּנִזָּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion and returns to analyze the ברייתא quoted earlier
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In property belonging only to the victim, the animal's owner is liable 'בכל', which the next step explains as full damage.

steps.title: "Liable in All" Means Full Damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא says "חייב בכל" and not "על הכל." It explains this to mean the owner pays the full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא does not say "liable for everything." It says "liable in all," meaning he pays the whole damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is reading the exact wording of the ברייתא's first rule. It shows that the rule is about how much the owner pays, not about which kinds of damage he is liable for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "על הכל" would mean he is liable for every type of damage. "בכל" means he pays all of it, meaning נזק שלם. So the ברייתא is saying that even damage that normally pays only half pays full here.

keyTerms.meaning: For everything (every type of damage)
In all (the full amount)
Damage
It does not teach

steps.confusionAlert: The two phrases sound almost the same in English. "על הכל" is about WHICH damages, while "בכל" is about HOW MUCH is paid.

phrases.english: It does not teach "for everything,"
phrases.notes: That wording would mean he is liable for every kind of damage.

phrases.english: rather, "he is liable in all":
meaning, for the whole damage.
phrases.notes: Some versions add the letter in square brackets; it doesn't change the meaning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the wording of the first rule just quoted in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the victim's property, the owner pays full damage, even for a type of damage that usually pays half.

steps.title: This Follows רבי טרפון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the ברייתא follows רבי טרפון, who holds that unusual goring (קרן) in the victim's courtyard pays full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion is this? It is רבי טרפון, who says that unusual goring in the victim's courtyard pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies whose opinion the ברייתא follows. It is רבי טרפון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally קרן by an animal that has not yet gored repeatedly pays only half. רבי טרפון holds that in the victim's own courtyard it pays full. That matches the reading of "חייב בכל" as full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose (opinion) is this?
The תנא who holds full payment for קרן in the victim's courtyard
Unusual behavior
Horn; the category of goring damage
Full damage payment

steps.whyThisMatters: It ties the ברייתא to one side of a known מחלוקת. So the ברייתא is not a general rule that everyone agrees with.

phrases.english: Whose view is this? It is רבי טרפון,
who says: Goring, which is unusual behavior,
in the courtyard of the injured one,
he pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the תנא whose view matches the full-damage reading from step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא follows רבי טרפון: unusual קרן in the victim's courtyard pays נזק שלם.

steps.title: Quoting the Last Part of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the סיפא. In a courtyard that belongs to neither party, the owner is liable for שן and רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the last part: in a place that is neither this one's nor that one's, like a courtyard that does not belong to both of them, he is liable there for Tooth and Foot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the end of the ברייתא. It is setting up a question about it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא describes a place that belongs to neither the damager nor the victim. It says the owner is still liable for שן (eating) and רגל (trampling). The גמרא is about to ask what kind of place this could be.

keyTerms.meaning: Say (look at) the last part
Not for this one and not for that one
Tooth; damage by eating
Foot; damage by trampling

phrases.english: Say the last part:
"Not for this one and not for that one,
such as a courtyard that does not belong to the two of them,

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בָּהּ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל.
phrases.english: he is liable in it for Tooth and for Foot."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first rule of the ברייתא to its last rule, to examine it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a courtyard belonging to neither party, the owner is liable for שן and רגל.

steps.title: Can the Courtyard Belong to an Outsider?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what "neither this one's nor that one's" means. If it means the place belongs to a third person, the פסוק "ובער בשדה אחר" is not fulfilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does "not for this one and not for that one" mean? If you say it belongs to neither of them at all, but to someone else, we need "and it ate in another's field," and that is missing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of courtyard the סיפא means. It rejects the simple reading that the courtyard belongs to a total outsider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability for שן and רגל comes from the פסוק "ובער בשדה אחר." That means the damage must happen in the victim's field. A field owned by a third person is not the victim's field, so the condition is missing, and there should be no liability.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (proposing a reading to reject it)
At all
Another person, an outsider
"And it ate in another's field": the source for liability of שן and רגל
And it is not there (the condition is missing)

steps.confusionAlert: Here "another's field" in the פסוק means the victim's field, not some third person's field. That is exactly why an outsider's courtyard does not work.

phrases.english: What does "not for this one and not for that one" mean?

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה כְּלָל –
phrases.english: If you say it is not for this one and not for that one at all,
but rather it belongs to someone else,
but we need "and it ate in another's field,"
and that is missing!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה״? אִילֵּימָא לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the case described in the סיפא quoted in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of the סיפא: that the courtyard belongs to a third person.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שן and רגל are liable only "בשדה אחר," meaning the victim's field. A third person's courtyard is not the victim's field, so liability should not apply.

steps.title: The place belongs to just one of them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא decides that 'neither this one's nor that one's' means the place is not owned by both together. It belongs to only one of them. It then quotes the last clause: a תם pays half damage and a מועד pays full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious: 'not this one's and not that one's' means it is not owned by both of them together. It belongs to one of them. And the last clause teaches: an innocuous ox pays half damage, and a forewarned ox pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question from the last step by explaining what kind of courtyard the ברייתא means. It then quotes the ruling about that courtyard, which sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 showed that the phrase cannot mean a third person's field. So the גמרא reads it as 'not owned by both together, but by one of them.' The ruling quoted for this case is that a תם pays only half damage, and that detail will create the next problem.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal without a history of goring (innocuous); it pays half damage for קרן
An animal that has been warned about (forewarned); it pays full damage
The last clause of a teaching
Half the value of the damage

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious
'not this one's and not that one's' means:
rather, it belongs to one of them;
and the last clause teaches:
an innocuous ox pays half damage,
and a forewarned ox pays full damage;

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא פְּשִׁיטָא, לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה – אֶלָּא דְּחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 21 about what 'neither this one's nor that one's' means.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase might mean a third person's field.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the place belongs to one of them, not to both together.

steps.title: The last clause matches the Rabbis
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that paying half damage for a תם in this courtyard is the view of the רבנן. The רבנן hold that unusual goring in the victim's courtyard pays only half.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we have arrived at the view of the רבנן, who say: unusual goring (קרן) in the victim's courtyard pays only half damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out whose opinion the last clause follows. This sets up a problem, because the first clause followed someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19 the first clause was shown to follow רבי טרפון, who makes קרן in the victim's courtyard pay full damage. Now the last clause says a תם pays half, which is the view of the רבנן. So the two clauses seem to follow two different opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the majority opinion arguing with רבי טרפון
Unusual behavior for the animal, like goring
The courtyard of the one who was damaged

phrases.english: We have arrived at the Rabbis, who say:
unusual goring in the victim's courtyard,
it is only half damage that he pays!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the ruling quoted in step 22, setting up a contrast with step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The last clause of the ברייתא follows the רבנן: unusual goring in the victim's courtyard pays half damage.

steps.title: Can one teaching follow two opinions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in surprise whether the first clause can follow רבי טרפון while the last clause follows the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first clause follows רבי טרפון, and the last clause follows the רבנן?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading it has built up. It seems strange for one ברייתא to switch opinions in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we expect one teaching to follow one consistent view. Here the רישא (step 19) matches רבי טרפון and the סיפא (step 23) matches the רבנן, and the גמרא questions whether that is acceptable.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a teaching
The תנא who holds that unusual goring in the victim's courtyard pays full damage

phrases.english: The first clause is Rabbi Tarfon,
and the last clause is the Rabbis?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the split that results from steps 19 and 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of the ברייתא that makes its two clauses follow different תנאים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A single ברייתא should follow one consistent opinion, not switch between רבי טרפון and the רבנן.

steps.title: Yes, as שמואל told רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes. A teaching can have a first clause following רבי טרפון and a last clause following the רבנן. שמואל explained a different משנה in exactly this way to רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. For שמואל said to רב יהודה: 'Sharp one, leave the משנה and follow me: the first clause is רבי טרפון, and the last clause is the רבנן.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the split reading. It brings proof that this kind of split already exists elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל already explained another משנה as following רבי טרפון in its first part and the רבנן in its last part. So it is not strange to read this ברייתא the same way, and the challenge from step 24 falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Sharp one', the name שמואל used for רב יהודה
Leave aside
After me, following my explanation

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר is split: its first clause follows רבי טרפון (full damage for unusual goring in the victim's courtyard), and its last clause follows the רבנן (half damage). שמואל's reading of another משנה shows that such a split is acceptable.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל's statement is not about this ברייתא. It comes from a different משנה, and the גמרא uses it only to show that a split teaching like this is acceptable.

phrases.english: Yes;

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: for Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda:
phrases.notes: This was said about a different משנה (on 15b), not this ברייתא.

phrases.english: Sharp one,
leave the mishna
and come after me:
phrases.notes: He means: drop your reading of the משנה and follow my explanation.

phrases.english: the first clause is Rabbi Tarfon,
and the last clause is the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין; דְּהָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24 by accepting the split reading and bringing a precedent.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a single teaching can follow different opinions in different clauses. The גמרא accepts this when the wording requires it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepting the challenged reading and supporting it with a precedent
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A single ברייתא cannot follow two different opinions.
steps.terutzMaskana: It can. שמואל explained another משנה the same way, with the first clause following רבי טרפון and the last following the רבנן.

steps.title: רבינא: The whole teaching follows רבי טרפון
steps.stepSummary: רבינא, in the name of רבא, says the whole ברייתא follows רבי טרפון. He reads 'not this one's and not that one's' as follows: for produce, only one person may use the place, but for oxen, both may use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said in the name of רבא: The whole teaching is רבי טרפון. What does 'not for this one and not for that one' mean? It is not shared by both for keeping produce. Only one of them may keep produce there. But both of them may keep their oxen there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new way to read the ברייתא. With his reading, we no longer need to split it between רבי טרפון and the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer said the first clause follows רבי טרפון and the last clause follows the רבנן. רבינא redefines the shared place: it belongs to one person for produce, but to both people for oxen. This sets up why the last clause can also fit רבי טרפון.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, meaning the whole teaching
Produce, fruit
Oxen
Belongs to one person

phrases.english: Ravina said in the name of Rava:
The whole teaching is Rabbi Tarfon's view;
and what does "not for this one and not for that one" mean?
Not for this one and that one together, for produce,
rather it belongs to one of them;
phrases.notes: Only the injured person may keep his produce there.

phrases.english: but it is for this one and for that one, for oxen.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר: כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the problem in step 24, replacing the 'split teaching' answer of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (the place is owned differently for produce and for oxen)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The last clause, where a תם pays half, must follow the רבנן, so the teaching is split.
steps.terutzMaskana: The place is shared for oxen, so the whole ברייתא can follow רבי טרפון.

steps.title: Eating counts as the victim's yard; goring counts as public
steps.stepSummary: Since only the victim keeps produce there, damage by eating counts as damage in the victim's courtyard. Since both keep oxen there, damage by goring counts as damage in a public area.
steps.simpleTranslation: So for damage by eating (שן), the place counts as the courtyard of the injured person. For damage by goring (קרן), it counts as a public area.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא applies his reading to the two kinds of damage. This shows how the whole ברייתא fits רבי טרפון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal eating produce is in a place that belongs only to the victim, so the owner is liable. For goring, both owners have a right to be there, so it is like a public area. Even רבי טרפון agrees that a תם pays only half there.

keyTerms.meaning: Tooth: damage from an animal eating
Horn: damage from goring
The courtyard of the injured person

phrases.english: So with regard to tooth (eating),
it counts as the courtyard of the injured party;
with regard to horn (goring),

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְגַבֵּי שֵׁן הָוְיָא לַהּ חֲצַר הַנִּיזָּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the legal results from רבינא's new definition in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The same place is the victim's courtyard for שן and a public area for קרן, so a תם gores there for half damage even according to רבי טרפון.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבינא, one place can have two legal identities. For eating, it is the victim's courtyard. For goring, it is a public area.

steps.title: Then there are only three rules, not four
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if רבינא is right, the ברייתא's fourth rule teaches nothing new. So the ברייתא should list only three rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, does it say four? There are only three!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's reading. With his reading, the fourth rule just repeats things we already know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first rule already says that one is liable for eating in a place set aside for the victim. The third rule already says that goring in a shared place pays half. So under רבינא's reading, the fourth rule adds nothing, and counting 'four' makes no sense.

phrases.notes: The ברייתא counts four rules, but on this reading the fourth just repeats the first three.

phrases.english: There are only three!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבינא's reading from steps 26–27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's explanation that the whole ברייתא follows רבי טרפון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A list of four rules should not include one that repeats the others. Under רבינא's reading, the fourth rule repeats the first and third rules, so there would really be only three.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק begins his answer
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק is introduced to answer the question of 'four or three.' His actual words come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next move. רב נחמן בר יצחק is about to answer why the ברייתא counts four rules, and his words continue right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the name of the speaker appears here. What he actually explains comes in the next lines of the גמרא.
